graphics.title: Control Line Breaks
graphics.mechanism: Choose where text continues onto a new line so phrasing, meaningful expressions and paragraph endings support the reading task without sacrificing adaptable layout.
graphics.reading: Text-like rows retain a shared starting edge while a bent accent arrow indicates a deliberate continuation onto a new line. The intervention changes the boundary rather than the letter size or line interval.

graphics.title: Use Type as Image
graphics.mechanism: Make letterforms, their arrangement or their interior spaces carry a relevant visual idea while preserving an appropriate route to reading the message.
graphics.reading: A recognizable U retains its open top and curved base while a small handle lets the same letter also suggest a vessel.

graphics.title: Establish Value Contrast
graphics.mechanism: Adjust light-dark relationships so necessary text, boundaries and priorities separate from their surroundings, without giving every element maximum contrast.
graphics.reading: A filled region and open outlined region share a central edge. The mark represents visible separation between tonal fields in the library palette rather than a measured color specimen.

graphics.title: Reinforce Meaning Beyond Color
graphics.mechanism: Give color-coded information another visible carrier, such as words, shapes or line patterns, so the intended meaning remains available without identifying the hue.
graphics.reading: A circle and triangle differ in form as well as library color. The two identities remain distinguishable from their outlines when hue is unavailable; the article supplies meaningful labels and mappings.

graphics.title: Choose Images for Meaning
graphics.mechanism: Select imagery for the specific activity, feature, subject or association the viewer needs to understand, and check that its visible content supports the surrounding message without implying unsupported facts.
graphics.reading: A framed image carries a small accent check. The mark represents selecting visual content for a defined communication job rather than changing its size or frame.

graphics.title: Crop for Impact
graphics.mechanism: Adjust the visible window within an image to emphasize useful content, protect important outlines and retain necessary context, while keeping the framing truthful to its purpose.
graphics.reading: Crossing right-angle guides define a retained rectangle. Their extensions recall a crop tool and distinguish the chosen window from the complete source.

graphics.title: Integrate Text and Image
graphics.mechanism: Coordinate the meaning, placement and connections of words and pictures so viewers can understand what belongs together while each remains useful and readable.
graphics.reading: A framed image and two text lines form a pair. An accent elbow connects text to a point within the image, making their reference explicit.

graphics.title: Simplify Through Abstraction
graphics.mechanism: Replace incidental appearance with selected shapes, relationships or steps that preserve the information needed for a particular recognition or understanding task.
graphics.reading: An irregular outlined form with internal marks becomes a simple bounded form. The connecting accent indicates a deliberate change of representation while a central internal feature survives.

graphics.title: Use Visual Metaphors
graphics.mechanism: Borrow a recognizable quality or relationship from one subject to communicate another, making the intended comparison clear and checking the implications it brings with it.
graphics.reading: A sprout joins an open book: the book is treated as a growing medium, suggesting development of ideas rather than merely depicting reading material.

graphics.title: Employ Recognizable Symbols
graphics.mechanism: Use visual signs whose meanings the intended audience can already recognize, match them to the actual service or action, and add words where the meaning remains uncertain.
graphics.reading: A familiar circled i supplies an information cue while a separate accent line stands for a confirming text label. It represents using a convention with words, not universal recognition.

graphics.title: Five-Minute Technique
graphics.mechanism: Commit to five minutes of a task, then decide whether to continue using what the attempt reveals.
graphics.reading: A short accented starting segment reaches an ink decision point, with three equally weighted gray paths beyond it for continuing, stopping, or adjusting.

graphics.title: Urge Surfing
graphics.mechanism: Notice an urge as a changing experience, allowing it to be present while choosing whether and how to respond.
graphics.reading: An ink wave remains present above a separate accented route and decision point, showing that a response can be chosen while the urge remains.

graphics.title: Establish Visual Hierarchy
graphics.mechanism: Choose what should lead, assign supporting levels of importance, and give recurring roles dependable visual treatments.
graphics.reading: Each row repeats the same treatment across two elements. A heavy green pair leads, a medium ink pair supports, and a thin ink pair provides a quieter level. Consistency within roles matters as well as distinction between them; three levels illustrate a case, not a universal rule.

graphics.title: Use Spacing to Express Relationships
graphics.mechanism: Allocate open space, relative distances and repeatable intervals so the layout expresses which elements belong together and where useful pauses occur.
graphics.reading: Each pair has a small internal gap; a larger central interval separates the two groups. Matching marks occur in both pairs, so proximity supplies local membership while shared appearance connects their roles.

graphics.title: Build a Purposeful Palette
graphics.mechanism: Choose a working set of colors whose unity, variation and distinctions serve the communication, while preserving necessary tonal separation.
graphics.reading: A compact palette card repeats a dark swatch and retains one contrasting accent, suggesting deliberate reuse rather than a unique color for each item. The number of pictured swatches is illustrative, not a universal limit.

graphics.title: Negative Visualization
graphics.mechanism: Anticipate a possible difficulty and consider a prepared, principled response.
graphics.reading: A direct route meets a possible obstruction. A green alternate route makes a prepared response visible while keeping the intended destination.

graphics.title: Adversity as Training
graphics.mechanism: Use an unwelcome situation to practise a specific quality of character.
graphics.reading: The ascending steps present a difficulty that can be used deliberately. Three green marks identify chosen efforts along the route, without promising an external result.

graphics.title: Dichotomy of Control
graphics.mechanism: Distinguish your contribution from an outcome that depends on more than your choices.
graphics.reading: A bounded green action sits inside a clear decision boundary. A gray outcome beyond the boundary is connected to the action while remaining outside its enclosure.

graphics.title: Pause Before Assent
graphics.mechanism: Examine an impression before accepting its interpretation or acting on its urgency.
graphics.reading: An incoming impression reaches a visible pause before a considered outgoing judgment. The gap and green pause bars interrupt the direct path from impression to conclusion.

graphics.title: Voluntary Discomfort
graphics.mechanism: Choose a modest inconvenience to examine dependence on a particular comfort.
graphics.reading: A smaller chosen green space remains within a larger boundary. The open return path shows that a voluntary experiment is limited and can end.

graphics.title: The View from Above
graphics.mechanism: Widen attention across space or time to restore proportion and recognize other lives.
graphics.reading: A green local concern appears within successively wider frames. Its position is retained while the surrounding context becomes visible.

graphics.title: Establish a Shared Visual Language
graphics.mechanism: Define dependable visual roles across related artifacts, deciding which features stay consistent and which may vary with content, format and use.
graphics.reading: Three differently proportioned frames retain the same accent square and text strokes. The repeated roles belong to one family while the artifact formats remain different.

graphics.title: Develop Distinctive Visual Cues
graphics.mechanism: Select and repeat identity features that remain distinguishable among relevant alternatives, survive their viewing conditions and build a dependable association with their source.
graphics.reading: Three equal frames share the same text strokes. The first two contain overlapping square cues; the third contains contrasting opposing corners, distinguishing one source among similar neighbors.

graphics.title: Build Reusable Templates
graphics.mechanism: Define editable content roles, required information and tested layout responses so recurring materials can accept new inputs without reconstructing the design or losing meaning.
graphics.reading: One source frame branches into two editions. All retain the same accent header, while the content lines have different lengths; reusable rules support changing content.

graphics.title: Barbell Strategy
graphics.mechanism: Protect a dependable base while reserving a bounded share of resources for uncertain opportunities with substantial potential upside.
graphics.reading: A large ink circle and a smaller green circle occupy opposite ends of a gray bar; the size contrast represents a protected base and a bounded exploratory allocation without prescribing a ratio.

graphics.title: Layers
graphics.mechanism: Organize responsibilities into ordered abstractions with explicit rules for which layers may use others.
graphics.reading: Three distinct stacked bands form ordered abstractions; the green middle service and short downward connectors show that an upper responsibility reaches a lower one through an explicit boundary.

graphics.title: Ports and Adapters
graphics.mechanism: Define application-owned ports for meaningful interactions and connect external technologies through replaceable adapters.
graphics.reading: A bounded core contains one operation; green contacts on its edge connect separate external blocks. The contacts belong to the core while the adapters remain outside.

graphics.title: Microkernel
graphics.mechanism: Keep a stable operational core and add specialized capabilities through plug-ins governed by explicit extension contracts.
graphics.reading: A bounded ink core contains the common workflow. Three separate green blocks connect at its edges, expressing optional capabilities attached through a shared extension surface rather than changes inside the core.

graphics.title: Pipes and Filters
graphics.mechanism: Decompose processing into independent filters connected by one-way streams, with each stage consuming the previous stage's output.
graphics.reading: Three bounded filters connect through right-pointing arrows. A small input block becomes a taller intermediate value and then output lines, expressing successive transformations rather than a choice of handler.

graphics.title: Blackboard
graphics.mechanism: Let independent knowledge sources build partial solutions in a shared workspace while a controller selects useful contributions from its current state.
graphics.reading: Three separate specialist blocks connect to a bounded shared workspace containing partial entries. A green controller below commits a contribution, expressing shared-state cooperation with separate control rather than a fixed chain of calls.

graphics.title: Modular Monolith
graphics.mechanism: Organize one deployable application into cohesive modules with explicit public interfaces and ownership of internal code and data.
graphics.reading: One ink boundary encloses two distinct modules. Their green public surfaces connect through a local arrow, while separate interior lines express privately owned state within a single application release.

graphics.title: Microservices
graphics.mechanism: Divide an application into independently deployable services around business capabilities, with explicit communication contracts and ownership of their data.
graphics.reading: Two separate service boundaries each contain a green public contract and private records. An inter-service arrow crosses the gap, without an enclosing application release boundary.

graphics.title: Dependency Injection
graphics.mechanism: Supply a component's collaborators from outside so it can use their contracts without choosing or constructing their implementations.
graphics.reading: An external assembly block supplies a green collaborator into an open consumer slot. A separate operational arrow connects the consumer to that collaborator, expressing external wiring rather than lookup or internal construction.

graphics.title: Functional Core, Imperative Shell
graphics.mechanism: Keep decisions and transformations in pure functions over values, while an outer shell gathers inputs and performs effects from their results.
graphics.reading: A green central computation receives and returns small value marks between two gray external-effect blocks. An outer ink boundary expresses the application shell while the green core owns decisions and no I/O.

graphics.title: Domain Model
graphics.mechanism: Organize business rules and state into collaborating domain objects whose operations preserve the model's invariants.
graphics.reading: Two caller blocks feed one green operation boundary on a domain object. The object encloses its owned reservation records, expressing shared behavior and invariant protection rather than independent callers editing rows.

graphics.title: Entity
graphics.mechanism: Track a domain object by a stable identity across changes and representations, rather than defining it by its current attributes.
graphics.reading: Two distinct object boundaries carry the same green identity bar while different ink detail marks indicate changed descriptive state. A connecting line links their common identity rather than merging their attributes or runtime instances.

graphics.title: Value Object
graphics.mechanism: Represent a meaningful domain value as an immutable whole, with equality determined by its attributes and operations that return new values.
graphics.reading: Two separate square boundaries contain matching green component bars and identical ink value marks. A central equals sign expresses equivalence of the complete value without an identity arrow or shared-object requirement.

graphics.title: Aggregate
graphics.mechanism: Group domain objects that must stay consistent behind one root, and make that boundary the unit of controlled change and atomic persistence.
graphics.reading: An outer square encloses a green root and two smaller owned values. A single incoming arrow ends at the root; internal connecting lines show its control of the contained values, rather than allowing direct outside writes to them.

graphics.title: Domain Service
graphics.mechanism: Express a meaningful domain operation that has no natural entity or value-object owner as a focused, stateless service with a domain-language contract.
graphics.reading: Three separate candidate squares feed a central green operation. One outgoing arrow ends at a distinct result square, expressing a decision over supplied participants without making the operation the owner of their continuing state.

graphics.title: Domain Event
graphics.mechanism: Represent a meaningful occurrence in the domain as an immutable fact, so its owner can record what happened without knowing every reaction.
graphics.reading: A small transition marker points to a distinct green fact square. Two outgoing branches terminate at independent reaction squares, keeping the occurrence separate from each reaction and from any transport or persistence guarantee.

graphics.title: Specification
graphics.mechanism: Give a domain matching rule its own object, so callers can reuse and combine the criterion independently of candidates and selection code.
graphics.reading: Two caller squares connect to one green criterion. A separate candidate square feeds that criterion and a small outgoing decision mark indicates the Boolean result, preserving the separation between matching requirements, candidate data, and caller actions.

graphics.title: Bounded Context
graphics.mechanism: Give each business model an explicit boundary for its terms and rules, then connect models through deliberate mappings rather than assuming shared meanings.
graphics.reading: Two distinct model boundaries each contain their own local shapes. A green translation bridge connects their interfaces without merging the contained models or their identities, expressing coherent local meaning and deliberate cross-boundary relationships.

graphics.title: Build a Scale from Steps
graphics.mechanism: Choose a repeatable pattern of pitch distances to give a melody a coherent note palette.
graphics.reading: Unequal gaps form the same ascending seven-step shape in two rows, preserving scale relationships at different starting pitches.

graphics.title: Service Layer
graphics.mechanism: Define application operations at a shared boundary that coordinates domain behavior, persistence, and transaction outcomes for different callers.
graphics.reading: Two separate client boxes converge through green call paths on one shared application-operation boundary. Three small marks within that boundary express coordinated steps, while the callers remain independent interfaces rather than duplicated use-case implementations.

graphics.title: Transaction Script
graphics.mechanism: Organize business logic around procedures that handle complete application requests, using direct data access or shared helpers as needed.
graphics.reading: One request enters a bounded procedure containing an ordered vertical series of decisions and updates. A green route connects the internal steps and exits as one result, expressing request-oriented business logic rather than a collaboration of stateful domain objects.

graphics.title: Repository
graphics.mechanism: Expose a domain-oriented collection of objects while keeping storage queries and mapping details behind a deliberate access contract.
graphics.reading: A caller approaches a green collection boundary through a single access path. Two alternative storage shapes sit behind it, each feeding the same domain-object result, expressing an access contract that hides storage-specific machinery rather than a particular database.

graphics.title: Data Mapper
graphics.mechanism: Move data between domain objects and database representations through a separate mapping layer, keeping persistence details out of the model.
graphics.reading: A nested object shape and a flat three-field row sit on opposite sides of a green mapping boundary. Two opposing paths express reconstruction and inverse writes, keeping the differently shaped representations connected without moving persistence knowledge into the domain object.

graphics.title: Active Record
graphics.mechanism: Put a row's data, domain behavior, and database access operations on the same object, giving callers a direct record-oriented API.
graphics.reading: One bounded record object contains a small data shape and two behavior marks. A green path leaves that same object for a row-shaped store below, expressing that record state, domain operations, and persistence knowledge belong to the same object rather than a separate mapper.

graphics.title: Unit of Work
graphics.mechanism: Track the objects affected by a business operation and coordinate their persistence changes within one explicit completion boundary.
graphics.reading: Three separately tracked object changes sit inside a scope and converge through a green coordination path on one database-write boundary. The grouping expresses pending new, modified, and removed work completed together rather than independently committed record calls.

graphics.title: Identity Map
graphics.mechanism: Keep one live object for each persistent identity within a defined scope, and reuse that object whenever the identity is loaded again.
graphics.reading: Two distinct upper lookup paths enter one outlined scope and converge on a single green reference that points to one lower object. The single target expresses shared local object identity; the enclosing boundary limits that promise to the scope.

graphics.title: Lazy Load
graphics.mechanism: Load the lightweight part of an object first, keeping a way to fetch its deferred data when that data is actually needed.
graphics.reading: A small solid compartment and a larger outlined compartment share one object boundary. A green demand path crosses the open side into the outlined portion, marking the point where omitted data is fetched. The differing compartments express lightweight initial data and deferred completion without implying a global cache.

graphics.title: Optimistic Offline Lock
graphics.mechanism: Retain the version read at the start of an edit, and accept its final write only if that version still matches in an atomic save transaction.
graphics.reading: Two proposal paths meet one central version gate. A green path passes the gate toward a changed record while the second stops against a gray boundary, expressing conditional acceptance of a still-current proposal and rejection of stale work.

graphics.title: Pessimistic Offline Lock
graphics.mechanism: Reserve write ownership before a long edit, retain that logical lock across requests, and validate ownership when saving or releasing it.
graphics.reading: A small ownership slot precedes a broad edit boundary. One green path occupies the slot and reaches the protected region; a second path stops before the reservation, expressing acquisition before work rather than conflict detection after editing.

graphics.title: Model-View-Controller
graphics.mechanism: Separate application state and rules, presentation of that state, and interpretation of user input so each responsibility can change without absorbing the others.
graphics.reading: Three separated boxes represent interaction, model state, and presentation. A green command path reaches the model, while a separate gray state path reaches the view. The missing closing triangle keeps this one-way teaching collaboration from claiming a universal MVC message cycle.

graphics.title: Model-View-Presenter
graphics.mechanism: Put a presenter between user gestures, application behavior, and screen updates so presentation decisions can be tested independently of GUI widgets.
graphics.reading: The left view connects to a central presenter; the presenter commands the model on the right and sends a separate lower display path back to the view. A parallel lower view box represents a recorder using the same output contract. There is no direct view/model link in this Passive View teaching variant.

graphics.title: Presentation Model
graphics.mechanism: Represent a screen's editable state, derived display properties, and actions in an object independent of widgets, then synchronize the view with that object.
graphics.reading: Three bounded boxes distinguish the view, the presentation model, and accepted domain data. Opposing view/model arrows stand for draft and action input versus property projection; the lower path reaches domain validation on Apply. A small inset inside the presentation box represents draft state rather than an additional accepted domain object.

graphics.title: Front Controller
graphics.mechanism: Channel a web application's requests through a common processing entry point, then delegate request-specific work to selected handlers.
graphics.reading: Three incoming paths converge on a shared bounded entry. A green dispatch path branches to separate delegates, and gray result paths join a lower completion boundary. The composition emphasizes a common lifecycle without replacing delegated business work or implying one physical server.

graphics.title: Template View
graphics.mechanism: Keep the shape of an HTML response in a template with markers for dynamic values, then render it with presentation data for the current request.
graphics.reading: Two independent upper boxes represent trusted template structure and request-specific values. Their green paths meet a bounded renderer, which produces a lower HTML page outline with three aligned content slots. The output is a projection of supplied values rather than a mutable domain object or inheritance hierarchy.

graphics.title: Unidirectional Data Flow
graphics.mechanism: Send interaction events to an explicit state owner, update state through a controlled path, and derive the UI from the resulting state.
graphics.reading: Four separated boxes form an event, update, state, and view cycle. Green arrowheads show the controlled forward path; a gray outer return path represents a new interaction event rather than direct backward state mutation. The open space separates these responsibilities without implying a global store or distributed ordering guarantee.

graphics.title: Publish-Subscribe
graphics.mechanism: Publish a message to a topic so independently interested subscribers can receive it without the publisher naming or calling each recipient.
graphics.reading: One incoming publication reaches a central topic boundary, then branches into three independent subscription boxes. Two smaller marks inside one subscription represent workers sharing that single workload; they do not add independent interests. Arrowheads express logical fan-out without promising durable or exactly-once business completion.

graphics.title: Request-Reply
graphics.mechanism: Pair a request message with a correlated reply so a caller can obtain an outcome without assuming that sending and receiving happen in one call stack.
graphics.reading: A requestor box and replier box are connected by two separately directed message paths. Matching small envelope marks on the outgoing request and returning answer indicate correlation. The return arrow goes to the requestor rather than a broadcast fan-out; matching does not promise remote success or cancellation.

graphics.title: Correlation Identifier
graphics.mechanism: Carry an explicit identifier across related messages so a receiver can recover the correct conversation context regardless of arrival order or individual message identity.
graphics.reading: Two separate message envelopes lead into a pending-context table. Matching small square marks on the envelopes and table rows express shared correlation while envelope outlines remain distinct. Directed paths indicate lookup rather than broadcast, ordering, guaranteed delivery, or remote exactly-once effects.

graphics.title: Content-Based Router
graphics.mechanism: Inspect a message's data and select the appropriate output channel, keeping destination-selection rules out of the producer and downstream handlers.
graphics.reading: One input envelope enters a square decision boundary containing three predicate strokes. Three possible output paths leave the boundary, but only one accent path leads to an emphasized output. The muted alternatives express available destinations rather than fan-out, and the highlighted result is route selection rather than confirmed business completion.

graphics.title: Message Translator
graphics.mechanism: Convert a message into the representation another application expects while making field mappings, units, meaning, and unsupported cases explicit at the integration boundary.
graphics.reading: One source envelope and one target envelope contain different field arrangements. Two directed association paths pass through a small conversion boundary; corresponding small identity marks remain aligned while larger measurement and code strokes change structure. This depicts a directional representation conversion, not routing to several consumers, semantic invention, or guaranteed delivery.

graphics.title: Anti-Corruption Layer
graphics.mechanism: Protect a local domain model by translating an external system's concepts, operations, and failures through an interface expressed in the local model's own terms.
graphics.reading: A local model box and an external model box meet through a distinct square boundary. Two differently arranged sets of concept strokes remain on their respective sides while one directed request and one returning-value path cross the boundary. The accent boundary indicates semantic isolation, not a firewall, automatic consistency, or proof that foreign status values equal local business facts.

graphics.title: Splitter
graphics.mechanism: Break a composite message into separately addressable messages so each meaningful part can be processed independently.
graphics.reading: One square parent containing two item strokes enters a smaller extraction boundary. Two separate directed paths lead to child boxes, each carrying one item stroke. The branches mean decomposition into distinct work, not broadcasting identical full messages, guaranteed worker ordering, or atomic publication.

graphics.title: Aggregator
graphics.mechanism: Hold related messages as a group, decide when the group is ready, and combine its contents into one meaningful result.
graphics.reading: Two separate member boxes flow into one square group boundary. The boundary holds distinct member strokes until its release condition is satisfied, then sends one directed output into a summary box. Converging paths signify grouping and combination, not guaranteed business success, a DDD root, broadcast forwarding, or atomic delivery.

graphics.title: Idempotent Receiver
graphics.mechanism: Make repeated deliveries of the same logical message leave the receiver's protected business state as if that message had been handled once.
graphics.reading: Two delivery paths enter one square receiver boundary. Inside, a processed-identity ledger and a business-state box share a single enclosing transaction. One output path leaves that boundary while the repeated delivery is recognized by the retained identity. The mark signifies protected local effects, not one network delivery, automatic ordering, or protection for external side effects.

graphics.title: Dead Letter Channel
graphics.mechanism: Move messages that leave the normal delivery or processing policy to a separate recovery channel, preserving evidence and ownership until their outcome is resolved.
graphics.reading: An input path reaches a decision boundary. One arrow continues along the normal channel while a second branches down into a separate square recovery store. The store retains original evidence and failure context; a distinct later path represents operator-controlled recovery. It indicates preserved unresolved work, not business completion, automatic retry cycles, or an unconditional guarantee of safe remote transfer.

graphics.title: Database per Service
graphics.mechanism: Keep each service's persistent data private to its owner, exposing business contracts instead of allowing other services to depend on its tables.
graphics.reading: Two service boxes sit above one large shared hosting boundary that contains two distinct private store boxes. Each service has its own directed SQL path to its store, while a separate service-to-service arrow crosses only the upper contract boundary. The shared enclosure indicates physical co-location, not permission to join or mutate another owner’s tables or a shared runtime transaction.

graphics.title: CQRS
graphics.mechanism: Separate the model that handles business changes from the model that answers queries, so each can serve its own responsibilities without forcing one representation to do both.
graphics.reading: Two input boxes lead to differently structured model boxes. The command model has a rule boundary and a directed read/write path, while the query model has flat result strokes and a distinct SELECT path. Both paths reach one shared store. The separation concerns conceptual responsibility, not mandatory separate databases, services, queues, Event Sourcing, or automatic eventual consistency.

graphics.title: Event Sourcing
graphics.mechanism: Make accepted business events the authoritative record and reconstruct state by applying them in order, keeping replay separate from repeated external actions.
graphics.reading: Three ordered event boxes form an authoritative history. A directed replay path leads into a derived state box, whose contents can be reconstructed. An expected-revision gate protects appends. The mark distinguishes authoritative facts from a replaceable projection, without implying notifications are repeated during replay.

graphics.title: Transactional Outbox
graphics.mechanism: Save an outgoing message with its business change in one database transaction, then relay committed messages with duplicate handling.
graphics.reading: One square transaction frame encloses a business record and a pending message. A directed path crosses the commit boundary into a relay and then a separate destination. The repeated message route retains its identity, distinguishing local atomic intent from possibly repeated delivery and separate receiver effects.

graphics.title: Saga
graphics.mechanism: Coordinate a business operation as locally committed steps, with explicit recovery and compensating actions when the overall operation cannot complete.
graphics.reading: A forward path crosses three separate participant boxes. After a refusal, a recovery path visits compensating operations for completed steps. A pause on the recovery path preserves unfinished work, distinguishing explicit business repair from a global rollback and avoiding a promise that all effects disappear.

graphics.title: API Composition
graphics.mechanism: Answer a cross-service query by calling the APIs that own the required data and joining their responses into one result.
graphics.reading: A query composer calls separate owner API boxes and receives their bounded result rows. Two response paths converge into a joined result with explicit key matches. No path reaches a private table, and the shared result boundary does not imply a shared snapshot or cross-service transaction.

graphics.title: Leader Election
graphics.mechanism: Select one participant to hold a coordination role for an authority term, with explicit rules for replacement and for rejecting obsolete authority.
graphics.reading: Three voter boxes form a fixed membership. Two vote paths converge on one elected role, while the third remains outside the winning set. A later authority path reaches a protected destination, whose retained guard rejects the older term. Selection, destination handover, and stopping the old process remain distinct responsibilities.

graphics.title: Lease
graphics.mechanism: Grant a scoped right for a limited time, renew it explicitly, and allow reassignment when that grant expires.
graphics.reading: A scoped grant sits above a time interval with an exclusive end boundary. A renewal path extends its lifetime before that end. A later acquisition has a separate identity. Expiry changes permission rather than stopping the previous process.

graphics.title: Reactor
graphics.mechanism: Wait for readiness across registered event sources, then dispatch short handlers that perform nonblocking work and return control to the loop.
graphics.reading: Two registered handle boxes feed one readiness selector and dispatcher. Its callback arrow reaches the matching handler, while a return path brings control back to the loop. The handler performs nonblocking I/O and retains per-connection state; readiness is not presented as a complete record.

graphics.title: Proactor
graphics.mechanism: Initiate asynchronous operations with request context, then dispatch their completion results to handlers that decide the next step.
graphics.reading: An initiator sends a request into the operation processor. A separate result path enters a completion queue and reaches the request’s matched handler. The operation happens before the handler consumes its outcome; request identity and lifetime remain explicit rather than treating completion as readiness.

graphics.title: Active Object
graphics.mechanism: Turn method invocations into queued requests and execute them through an object's scheduler, keeping its state under one execution owner and returning results separately.
graphics.reading: A caller-facing proxy creates queued method requests. A single owner path passes through a scheduler into servant state, while a separate result path resolves the future already returned to the caller. Queued invocation, owner-thread execution, and observation of results remain separate responsibilities.

graphics.title: Monitor Object
graphics.mechanism: Encapsulate shared state behind synchronized methods, using a monitor lock for exclusive access and condition waiting for state-dependent progress.
graphics.reading: Two caller boxes enter one monitor boundary. Inside it, a shared lock guards the protected state. A side loop denotes condition waiting that releases and reacquires the same lock before state rechecking. Calls execute on their callers rather than on an object-owned worker, and notification does not represent ownership transfer.

graphics.title: Producer-Consumer
graphics.mechanism: Separate work creation from execution through a synchronized buffer, with explicit capacity, ownership, and completion rules.
graphics.reading: One producer feeds a two-place queue. Two outgoing branches lead to independent consumers; each queued entry is taken by one consumer, rather than broadcast to both. A reference lane separates waiting places from active processing. The producer waits when the queue is full and each consumer continues its own execution outside the queue lock.

graphics.title: Thread Pool
graphics.mechanism: Reuse a managed group of worker threads to execute submitted tasks, separating task lifetime from thread creation and shutdown.
graphics.reading: One admission window tracks task futures above two worker lanes. Each lane contains two successive task boxes joined along the same worker thread, making thread reuse distinct from task creation. The window limits uncollected work while the pair limits active execution; a task finishing does not destroy its worker or release a coordinator slot before collection.

graphics.title: Resource Pool
graphics.mechanism: Manage reusable resources behind a borrowing boundary, returning each to circulation only after exclusive use and required cleanup.
graphics.reading: A pool boundary contains two resource slots. Outgoing paths grant each slot to a distinct borrower, while a separate incoming path returns an instance through a reset box before it can rejoin availability. Physical resource lifetime spans several scoped borrowers; a previous borrow handle does not regain access when the instance is reused.

graphics.title: Scoped Locking
graphics.mechanism: Bind an acquired lock's release to a scope so normal exits, early returns, and exceptions cannot omit the matching unlock.
graphics.reading: One lock entry leads into a protected body. Normal, return and exception branches converge at one release boundary before reaching the caller. The multiple outgoing branches are mutually exclusive control-flow exits, not repeated releases or automatic data rollback.

graphics.title: Scoped Resource Management
graphics.mechanism: Give each acquired resource a deterministic owner that releases it when its scope ends, including during failure and partial acquisition.
graphics.reading: Three successful acquisitions enter one ownership scope from top to bottom. A separate exit path releases those resources bottom to top before a detached result leaves. The scope owns cleanup obligations; a wrapper can borrow its underlying resource.

graphics.title: Timeout
graphics.mechanism: Limit how long an operation may wait, then take an explicit failure path without assuming that the underlying work stopped or had no effect.
graphics.reading: Two sequential stages consume one horizontal allowance ending at a fixed deadline. A branch at that boundary leaves toward expiry; a separate continuation represents work that may remain active beyond the caller’s wait. The mark distinguishes an expired wait from proof that execution stopped.

graphics.title: Exponential Backoff with Jitter
graphics.mechanism: Increase retry wait limits after eligible failures and randomize each wait, spreading recovery traffic while keeping attempts and total elapsed time bounded.
graphics.reading: Three context rows share the same time direction. Accent marks move to different positions within wider successive timing ranges, representing independently jittered retry starts rather than repeated synchronized columns. A boundary at the right represents finite policy limits, not unlimited recovery or guaranteed completion.

graphics.title: Circuit Breaker
graphics.mechanism: Temporarily reject new calls to an unhealthy dependency, then admit limited recovery probes before allowing normal traffic again.
graphics.reading: Three square states form an admission lifecycle. The first admits normal work, the second interrupts it, and the third grants a limited probe. Separate return paths take a successful probe back to normal admission or a failed probe back to rejection. State changes do not represent retries, queueing or cancellation of earlier calls.

graphics.title: Bulkhead
graphics.mechanism: Partition constrained capacity into separately enforced compartments so overload in one workload or dependency cannot consume every compartment's allowance.
graphics.reading: Three square capacity compartments have separate boundaries. The center compartment’s slots are full while the outer compartments retain their own allowances. This represents resource-scoped admission rather than a shared unrestricted pool; it does not imply CPU, thread, security or data isolation.

graphics.title: Queue-Based Load Leveling
graphics.mechanism: Buffer bursty requests in a queue and control the aggregate drain so downstream work proceeds within a sustainable budget.
graphics.reading: Three job outlines wait inside a square buffer while a narrow exit leads to one separate completed-job square. An incoming arrow points into the buffer and an outgoing arrow shows controlled work transfer. The queue stores pending demand; the exit represents separately controlled aggregate consumption, not automatic capacity or guaranteed business completion.

graphics.title: Backpressure
graphics.mechanism: Slow or pause upstream admission when downstream work cannot keep up, using feedback to bound buffering instead of letting queues grow without control.
graphics.reading: Three square stages carry work left to right along a forward arrow. A lower return arrow points from the receiver back toward the source, showing that downstream capacity controls further admission. Separate directions distinguish data delivery from capacity permission; the mark does not imply durable completion, automatic total-memory limits or extra processing capacity.

graphics.title: Load Shedding
graphics.mechanism: Refuse selected work before expensive processing when an admission policy says available capacity cannot safely accommodate it.
graphics.reading: An incoming request reaches a square admission gate and branches toward either a protected work box or a separate refusal box. The refusal path ends before the protected work boundary. This represents deliberate admission loss, not a queue, automatic retry, priority reservation or cancellation of previously running work.

graphics.title: Health Endpoint
graphics.mechanism: Expose a small, explicit health contract that an external observer can use to make routing, startup, or recovery decisions.
graphics.reading: A separate observer box exchanges a request and a result with an instance boundary containing a small health endpoint. A separate lower policy box belongs to the observer. This distinguishes reported health evidence from the external routing or recovery action; the endpoint is not a universal business-correctness proof or a controller that restarts itself.

graphics.title: Cache-Aside
graphics.mechanism: Let application code check a disposable cache first, load misses from the authoritative store, and manage invalidation after writes.
graphics.reading: An application at the left has separate lookup paths to the cache above and authoritative source below at the right. The upper lookup can return a reusable value; the lower source access is needed on a miss. A separate upward accent path starts at the application and marks application-managed cache fill. No backend is drawn as owning access to the other.

graphics.title: Memoization
graphics.mechanism: Remember a function’s completed results under equivalent inputs so later calls can reuse them instead of repeating the calculation.
graphics.reading: Two separate upper dependency boxes request the same lower subproblem result. The lower box is shared and accented; its horizontal internal rule represents a completed memo entry. Arrows mean needs this subproblem result, not a broadcast or sequential execution. The concept mark shows reuse within one problem scope rather than cross-snapshot identity.

graphics.title: Materialized View
graphics.mechanism: Store a query’s derived result for reuse, with explicit maintenance and freshness rules that keep consumers aware of when the stored answer is valid.
graphics.reading: Source records at the left feed a separate stored derived relation at the right through a labeled-in-article maintenance lifecycle. The green arrow denotes materialization/refresh rather than query-time recomputation. The right-hand box contains two horizontal result rows and is distinct from the source record boxes. Publication/freshness rules belong to the mechanism; the mark does not promise automatic incremental maintenance.

graphics.title: Sharding
graphics.mechanism: Distribute rows across independently operated shards and route requests to their owners, increasing capacity while making cross-shard work and resharding explicit responsibilities.
graphics.reading: An input key at the left reaches a placement junction, which selects one of three separate row stores. The accent path ends only at the middle shard; grey branches denote other possible ownership paths. Each store has the same row structure but represents a different subset, not three replicas. Routing choice, logical partition ownership and safe movement are explained in the article.

graphics.title: Competing Consumers
graphics.mechanism: Let interchangeable workers share one logical work channel so each delivery goes to one worker, increasing concurrent processing while keeping redelivery and completion explicit.
graphics.reading: Three waiting job rows share one queue at the left. Separate green arrows leave two different row positions and reach distinct consumer boxes at the right. This divides logical jobs across interchangeable receivers rather than copying one publication to every interest. The remaining row represents waiting work. Redelivery and business completion remain separate contracts explained in the article.

graphics.title: Batching
graphics.mechanism: Group compatible operations into bounded execution units to share fixed overhead, with explicit limits on size, waiting, and completion semantics.
graphics.reading: Three separate operation boxes on the left feed one bounded envelope on the right through a single green grouping arrow. Three internal rows remain distinct inside that envelope, so shared execution does not imply combining business meaning or an atomic transaction. Count, byte, age and shutdown limits control when the unit is handed off; the article explains service overhead and separate result ownership.

graphics.title: Request Coalescing
graphics.mechanism: Let overlapping callers for an equivalent operation share one in-flight execution, then retire that shared work without implying a completed-result cache.
graphics.reading: Two identical request representatives at the left join one central active-flight box, which starts one loader at the right. Green arrows distinguish joining an existing flight from starting its underlying execution. The two request boxes remain separate callers; the central box is one live operation, not a batch of distinct members or a completed-result cache. Scope, result sharing, cancellation and cleanup are explained in the article.

graphics.title: Reference Monitor
graphics.mechanism: Mediate every protected access through a policy-enforcing mechanism that cannot be bypassed or altered by its subjects and is small enough for convincing analysis.
graphics.reading: Two subject access paths enter the same bounded enforcement region. A compact central check stands before a separate protected resource. Only the green permitted-operation arrow reaches that resource; there is no direct caller-to-resource route in the depicted design. The enclosing boundary represents the required protection of mechanism and resource paths, not proof that a wrapper or Python class provides isolation. Three whole-design requirements and trusted administration are explained in the article.

graphics.title: Gatekeeper
graphics.mechanism: Screen public requests in a limited-privilege tier that forwards a narrow contract to private services holding the data access and business authority.
graphics.reading: A public caller reaches the narrow screening component first. Its selected-operation arrow enters a separate private boundary, where the service alone reaches the data store. The public adapter has no direct caller-to-store path or storage authority. Separate boxes represent deployment responsibilities and required privilege separation, not proof that two classes enforce isolation. The article separately explains service authentication and current end-user business authorization.

graphics.title: Federated Identity
graphics.mechanism: Accept authentication assertions from explicitly trusted identity providers, then resolve the federated identity to a local account whose access the application controls.
graphics.reading: Two separate identity-provider boxes supply assertions to one relying-party boundary. Green paths express the trusted authentication handoff; they converge on the RP component, not a claim that the providers share an account namespace. The RP holds local identity association and resource permission, shown as separate inner elements. Verification, issuer-qualified subjects and independent session/access lifetimes are explained in the article. The mark does not imply an unverified claim or matching email grants access.

graphics.title: Externalized Authorization
graphics.mechanism: Move access-decision policy behind a dedicated decision interface while keeping enforcement beside every protected operation.
graphics.reading: The application enforcement point on the left asks the separate policy decision point at upper right, then receives a decision on the return arrow. A distinct lower path from the enforcement point reaches the protected resource only after that decision is usable. There is no policy-engine-to-resource operation arrow: the evaluator supplies a decision rather than performing the read. The article explains trusted facts, strict permit handling, obligations, failure and policy freshness; the mark does not claim that logical component separation supplies process isolation.

graphics.title: Valet Key
graphics.mechanism: Authorize a client to obtain a short-lived, narrowly scoped grant that the resource service validates during direct data access.
graphics.reading: A client on the left exchanges an authorization request and a narrow grant with the issuer at upper right. A separate pair of arrows connects the client directly with storage at lower right for the resource request and bytes. There is no issuer-to-storage byte relay in the mark. Storage validates the grant while the issuer retains broad authority. Resource, method, time and bearer-possession limits are explained in the article; the mark does not imply single-use or universal revocation.

graphics.title: Test Double
graphics.mechanism: Replace a production collaborator with a test-controlled substitute to supply specific responses or observe interactions while exercising the real subject.
graphics.reading: The real subject stays on the left. The collaborator on the upper right is the production alternative; a second square on the lower right is the test-controlled replacement. Only the lower path is emphasized for the test. Two short strokes inside the replacement denote a configured response and a recorded observation; the mark does not imply the real provider is tested.

graphics.title: Test Data Builder
graphics.mechanism: Create real test inputs from reusable defaults while letting each test override the values that explain its scenario.
graphics.reading: A small recipe with three default strokes branches through two construction arrows into distinct result squares. Each result owns a separate interior line; there is no shared mutable child linking them. The lower result has a visible changed property. Defaults and selected differences belong to a test recipe while both results remain real input objects, not substitute collaborators or calculated expected answers.

graphics.title: Consumer-Driven Contract Tests
graphics.mechanism: Let consumers define executable expectations for the interfaces they actually use, then verify those expectations against provider changes before rollout.
graphics.reading: A consumer check on the left and provider check on the right connect through a small central agreement. Two separate outer boxes represent independently executed test contexts; the agreement is the common evidence, rather than a direct full-system runtime connection. The lower parallel strokes denote matching obligations and verification results. A passing check on only one side is insufficient; version and interaction scope are explained in the article.

graphics.title: Strangler Fig
graphics.mechanism: Replace a legacy system in useful slices through controlled seams, shifting responsibility to the new implementation while old and new coexist.
graphics.reading: One client entry on the left reaches a central routing seam. Two distinct outgoing routes reach the legacy block above and the replacement block below. Three capability marks remain in the old block while one matching capability is visibly displaced into the new block. This represents a mid-migration split of responsibility rather than automatic fallback or duplication of writes. The article separately explains data readiness, in-flight ownership and eventual retirement.

graphics.title: Expand–Migrate–Contract
graphics.mechanism: Introduce a replacement alongside the old interface, migrate data and consumers, then remove the old representation after verifying that dependencies have moved.
graphics.reading: A small old-only interface on the left becomes a larger middle interface containing two rows, then a small new-only interface on the right. The upper middle row matches the old mark; the lower row and final mark use the mechanism accent for the new form. Arrows show lifecycle progression, not concurrent execution or automatic deletion. The article makes consumer migration, state consistency and evidence-gated contraction explicit.

graphics.title: Branch by Abstraction
graphics.mechanism: Replace an implementation incrementally behind a shared abstraction, keeping the system releasable while old and new implementations coexist.
graphics.reading: Two callers feed a single horizontal abstraction boundary. Below it, branches reach an old supplier on the left and an accented replacement on the right. Arrows depict alternative call paths through the same seam, not required parallel execution. The article explains selection, coexistence checks and eventual retirement.

graphics.title: Feature Toggle
graphics.mechanism: Select between deployed behaviors through a configurable decision, so feature exposure can change independently of a code deployment.
graphics.reading: Two small upper boxes represent context and policy inputs. They meet at a central decision boundary. Two lower arrows lead to alternative behavior boxes; only the right replacement path uses the accent. The structure means evaluation selects one behavior, rather than executing both. The article explains request consistency, default behavior and retirement.

graphics.title: Blue-Green Deployment
graphics.mechanism: Prepare a release in a separate production-capable environment, then switch incoming traffic to it while retaining the previous environment for a controlled return.
graphics.reading: A stable router on the left has two possible routes to separate environment boxes on the right. The upper existing environment remains drawn in ink; the lower candidate route is accented. The paths show alternate traffic destinations, not duplicated requests. The article explains promotion, in-flight ownership, current-state return eligibility and eventual retirement.

graphics.title: Canary Release
graphics.mechanism: Give a candidate release a limited share of real traffic, evaluate release-specific evidence, and expand, hold, or restore the incumbent under explicit rules.
graphics.reading: A top router divides real work between two serving boxes. The candidate box and path use the mechanism accent. Both paths converge on a lower evidence gate, emphasizing that the release decision uses attributed serving evidence rather than elapsed time alone. Box widths do not encode allocation percentages. The article supplies expansion, bounded hold and restoration rules.

graphics.title: Deployment Pipeline
graphics.mechanism: Move a versioned release artifact through ordered validation and deployment stages, accumulating evidence before allowing promotion to the next environment.
graphics.reading: Four stages form a downward path. Each arrow passes a candidate to the next stage, while the accented third boundary represents the promotion gate. The article explains that evidence refers to one artifact identity and that stage success does not itself prove production safety.
